content: The Jatene procedure, also known as the arterial switch operation, is the preferred and most commonly utilized surgical method for correcting d-transposition of the great arteries (d-TGA). Ideally, this procedure is performed on infants between 8 and 14 days of age. The surgery involves accessing the heart and great vessels through a median sternotomy, and the patient is placed on a cardiopulmonary bypass machine. Since the bypass machine requires priming with blood, a blood transfusion is necessary for the procedure. During the operation, both the aorta and pulmonary artery are transected. The coronary arteries are carefully detached from the aorta and reattached to the newly constructed neo-aorta. Subsequently, the upper portions of the aorta and pulmonary artery are switched to their respective opposite arterial roots. Including the time required for anesthesia and immediate postoperative recovery, the entire surgery typically takes approximately six to eight hours to complete. Some patients who undergo the arterial switch procedure may develop postoperative pulmonary stenosis. This complication can be addressed through interventions such as balloon angioplasty, pulmonary stenting via cardiac catheterization, median sternotomy, or the use of a xenograft. In cases where an arterial switch procedure is not feasible—due to factors such as late diagnosis, sepsis, or an unfavorable coronary artery anatomy—alternative approaches are considered. For example, in the presence of sepsis or delayed diagnosis, a delayed arterial switch may sometimes be made possible by performing pulmonary artery banding (PAB), which may also require the construction of an aortic-to-pulmonary artery shunt. If an arterial switch is entirely unachievable, an atrial switch procedure is performed instead, using either the Senning or Mustard technique. Both of these methods involve creating a baffle to redirect oxygenated and deoxygenated blood to the appropriate arteries. Since the late 1970s, the Mustard procedure has been the preferred approach for atrial switch surgeries. Following corrective surgery, but prior to the cessation of anesthesia, two small incisions are made just below the sternotomy site to allow for the placement of chest tubes. These tubes facilitate the drainage of fluid from the thoracic cavity, with one tube positioned anteriorly and the other posteriorly to the heart. After surgery, the patient is transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) for recovery, maintenance, and close monitoring. The average recovery time in the ICU is approximately two weeks, after which the patient may be moved to a Transitional Care Unit (TCU) and eventually to a cardiac ward. Postoperative care is similar to the care provided during palliative management, with the exception that the patient no longer requires prostaglandin E (PGE) or palliative surgical procedures. Additionally, the patient is placed on a cooling blanket to prevent fever, which could lead to brain damage. The sternum is intentionally left open immediately after surgery to allow for extra space in the thoracic cavity, thereby reducing pressure on the heart, which tends to swell significantly following the procedure. The sternum and surgical incision are closed a few days later, once the swelling has sufficiently subsided.
